rationale: This ethnographic and historical legal-anthropological study (1965-2012) examines how statutory law, donor/national project bylaws (CIDA, GWSC, NCWSP), and customary norms interact via institutional bricolage to shape household water access in a Northern Ghana village. Multiple rule-type mechanisms are co-equally central: capital cost-sharing rules (the 5% community contribution), local entrance fees, borehole user fees, and monthly piped-water tariffs (fees_tariffs_subsidies) serve as the primary empirical barrier and focal site of local rule-making, alongside mandated formalization of water user committees and WSDBs (participation_assistance), shifts across private compound wells, centralized state utility management, church ownership, and community management (regulatory_model_ownership), formal membership boundaries tying compounds to single pumps (eligibility_status_documentation), system shutoff/pump removal for tariff non-payment (enforcement_sanctions), and informal customary non-exclusion and poverty fee exemptions (discretion_accommodation). Outcomes are likewise multi-dimensional, centering on source functionality, service continuity, waiting times, fetching distance, and water quantities (effective_access), alongside delivery or non-delivery of boreholes and piped infrastructure (primary_connection), affordability barriers (economic_access), and project application delays/cutoffs (administrative_outcome).
